name: Kira Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Kira, thanks for agreeing to this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or any political party. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a formwork crew, so we build the wooden and steel moulds that the concrete gets poured into. Right now it's a nine-storey apartment block by the ring road, and we're on level five. I cut and fix plywood panels, screw up the props, oil the faces so the concrete comes off clean, and then strip it all down again a few days later. Tomasz, our ganger, runs the crew, and I'm the newest of six.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's physical and simple, you can see if you've done it right. I did a year in a call centre before this and I nearly lost my mind staring at a screen, so I like that nobody makes me log in to anything. What wears me out is stripping out on a hot day, the panels are heavy and the concrete dust gets everywhere. My dad was a bricklayer, so he thinks I'm mad, but proud mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much, to be honest. Maybe at break I'd say, well, that's that then, and go back to my sandwich. I don't really post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays my job. I can keep learning formwork properly, get faster at reading the drawings, and maybe be a ganger like Tomasz in ten years. That's about all I want from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep turning up, keep putting a bit away. I've got about four months saved and I'm trying to get a deposit together for a better car, mine's sixteen years old and the clutch is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm, normal, like nothing happened, which is how I'd like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about AI now that bothers you, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that everyone keeps telling me I should use it. Mats, my boyfriend, has it on his phone for his delivery routes, and he keeps showing me things. I just don't see what it's for in my job, you can't ask a chatbot how tight a prop is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned wanting to be a ganger in ten years. What does that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly time and not messing up. You've got to read the drawings fast, know your loads, and keep six people moving without anyone getting hurt. I'm still slow on the drawings, Tomasz has to check my setting out, but I'll get there.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe just 'well, that's that then' at break. I don't really post things online.
S0.think: Privately it means her job stays her job, and she can keep learning formwork. Maybe she becomes a ganger like Tomasz in ten years.
S0.do: Keeps working on the formwork crew and keeps saving, with about four months put by. Saves towards a better car because hers is sixteen years old and the clutch is going.
S0.feel: Calm and normal, which is how she likes it.
S0.quote: I just don't see what it's for in my job, you can't ask a chatbot how tight a prop is.
S0.fieldNote: Kira likes her work precisely because it's physical and screen-free, after a bad year in a call centre. She is quiet, low-drama and not online. Her ambitions are modest and practical: a car that works and, in time, running a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will have to get on with it, like they always have. Some jobs go, some come. I'd probably say that to Mats and my dad, and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, formwork worries me. It's repetitive, the same panels over and over, and they already have factories that make whole concrete walls and bring them on a lorry. Tomasz showed me a video of a machine printing a concrete house, and I didn't sleep great that night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job as long as it's there and not go chasing anything. I'd stop spending on extras, no new car, and get my savings closer to six months. If the crew started getting smaller, I'd ask Tomasz what he thinks I should learn, because I trust him more than anyone on a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more than I'd show. I'd be fine on the outside and not fine at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people will have to get on with it. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes. But I know I'm the type who sits tight and hopes it passes me by, I did that at the call centre for a whole year before I left. So maybe I'd get on with it, just a bit late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there someone at work you'd worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, he's fifty-eight and his back's done. He only knows formwork, and he's not going to learn anything new now. If they cut the crew, he's first and I'm second, because I'm the newest.

S1.say: I'd say people will have to get on with it like they always have; some jobs go and some come. I'd say that to my boyfriend and my dad and leave it there.
S1.think: Privately formwork worries her because it's repetitive and factories already make whole concrete walls off site. A video of a printed concrete house kept her awake.
S1.do: Holds onto her job without chasing alternatives and drops the car plan to build savings towards six months. Plans to ask her ganger what to learn if the crew starts shrinking.
S1.feel: Anxious inside while looking fine on the outside, especially at three in the morning.
S1.quote: I'd be fine on the outside and not fine at three in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: Kira's calm public stance hides a clear private worry, because she sees formwork as repetitive and easy to move into factories. She's honest about her own habit of sitting tight too long. Her trust goes to her ganger, not to technology or institutions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something like, well, we're all in the same boat then. I'm not one for big opinions online. If anything, I'd say the government had better have a plan, because I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between you and me, I think I'm out of a job within the two years after it lands. Concrete moulds are about the easiest thing in building to hand to a machine. I left school without finishing, so it's not like I've got something else to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on everything but rent, food and petrol, and cancel the car plan for good. I'd ask Mats if we could move in together properly to save on rent, we've been putting that off. And I'd ask my dad if his mate's firm needs anyone for repairs and odd jobs, because old houses are fiddly and might be the last thing a robot does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a rug's being pulled and I can't see what's under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with Mats. Is that something you wanted anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, but not like that. I wanted to do it because we're ready, not because I'm scared of the rent. It'd feel like the robots made the decision for us, which is daft, but that's how it would feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Mats's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He drives a van, so he'd be worried too, maybe more. Self-driving vans are probably first. So it'd be two of us with four months of savings each and no clue, which is a horrible thought.

S2.say: I'd say we're all in the same boat then, and the government had better have a plan because I don't. I'm not one for big opinions online.
S2.think: Privately she expects to lose her job soon after it arrives, since concrete moulds are easy to hand to a machine. Without school certificates, she has nothing to fall back on.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent, food and petrol and drops the car plan. Asks her boyfriend Mats to move in together to save rent, and asks her dad's contacts about repair and odd-job work in old houses.
S2.feel: Alarmed, as if a rug is being pulled and she can't see what's underneath.
S2.quote: It'd feel like the robots made the decision for us, which is daft, but that's how it would feel.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture pushes her into immediate household moves, including moving in with her boyfriend for the wrong reasons, which clearly bothers her. Her partner's driving job makes the household doubly exposed. She looks to family networks rather than government or training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit of time, so people should use it. Get ready, don't moan about it. That's about what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps but I don't trust myself to use it. I'd tell myself next year, next year, like I did at the call centre. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, and I don't know what a thirty-two-year-old ex-formwork joiner does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, keep the job and keep saving, I'd aim for six months. By year two or three I'd try to move onto repair and renovation work, old houses, probably with Dad's mate, because it's still hands-on and it's not the same thing every day. I wouldn't do a computer course, I know that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Better than the fast one, but it's a slow ache instead of a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why repair work rather than something completely new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know wood and tools and I'm not starting from zero. Every old house is different, wonky walls, rotten joists you only find when you open it up. I reckon a robot would hate that, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a computer course. Even if that's where the work is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, no. I know that sounds stubborn. I'd rather do less money with my hands than more money sat in front of a screen, I tried that and it made me miserable.

S3.say: I'd say five years is some time, so people should use it to get ready instead of moaning. That's about all I'd say.
S3.think: Privately five years helps, but she doesn't trust herself to use it and fears putting it off. At thirty-two she doesn't know what an ex-formwork joiner does.
S3.do: Keeps the formwork job and builds savings to six months in the first year. Moves into old-house repair and renovation work by year two or three, likely through her dad's contacts, and avoids computer-based courses.
S3.feel: Anxious, like a slow ache instead of a punch.
S3.quote: I'd rather do less money with my hands than more money sat in front of a screen, I tried that and it made me miserable.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her a practical move: from repetitive formwork to irregular repair work in old houses. She openly rejects screen-based retraining because of her call centre year. Her biggest doubt is her own tendency to delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can happen. People should just keep an eye on it. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be thirty-seven. I'd hopefully be a ganger by then, or close. Then it comes and I'm a ganger of nothing, which isn't great, but that's a problem for future me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the first year I wouldn't change much. Keep working, keep saving, maybe buy the car after all. Somewhere around year five, if I'm seeing robots on sites, I'd look at the repair work idea from before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sort of in the background. Not enough to keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a problem for future me. Does that worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. My dad always says I leave things to the last minute, and he's right. But you can't plan ten years when you don't even know what you'll want next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz. If he said, Kira, you need to look at something else, I'd listen. Or if the crew went from six to four. Seeing actual people leave would do it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can happen, so people should just keep an eye on it. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.
S4.think: Privately she hopes to be a ganger by thirty-seven, then becomes 'a ganger of nothing'. She treats it as a problem for future her.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving in the first year and may buy the car after all. Plans to look at repair work around year five if robots appear on sites, or earlier if her ganger advises it or the crew shrinks.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, not enough to lose sleep.
S4.quote: Then it comes and I'm a ganger of nothing, which isn't great, but that's a problem for future me.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning lets Kira go back to life as normal, and she's aware that's partly avoidance. What would move her is people, not news: her ganger's advice or seeing the crew shrink. Her goal of becoming a ganger stays in place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Mats and I would both be hit at the same time with not much saved. What would help is someone telling us straight what work is left and paying us while we move into it. Not a website, an actual person on site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose that isn't money. On a pour day, when the concrete truck turns up and the whole crew's shouting and it all goes right, that's the best feeling I've had at work. I don't know what replaces that.

headlineQuote: On a pour day, when the concrete truck turns up and the whole crew's shouting and it all goes right, that's the best feeling I've had at work.
portrait: Kira Hansen is a 27-year-old junior formwork joiner on an apartment block, who left a call centre job because she couldn't stand screens. She lives with her boyfriend Mats, a van driver, has about four months saved and is quietly pragmatic, rarely posting opinions. She is calm if AI fizzles but already anxious with steady change, because formwork is repetitive and easy to move into factories. AGI in two years alarms her, with both her and Mats exposed. With more time she'd move into old-house repair work, but she admits she tends to leave things too late.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Mats would both be hit at once with little saved.
whatWouldHelp: Someone telling her straight what work is left, in person on site, and paying her while she moves into it.
